clinicalPearls: A benign sclerosing lesion with a fibroelastic core from which ducts and lobules radiate, termed a complex sclerosing lesion when larger than about 1 cm.
Usually impalpable and detected on screening mammography as a stellate or spiculated lesion that closely mimics invasive carcinoma.
The mammographic appearance may show a radiolucent centre and long radiating spicules, sometimes varying between projections ('black star').
Frequently harbours or is associated with atypical hyperplasia, in situ carcinoma or, less often, invasive carcinoma at its periphery.
Core biopsy sampling can under-represent associated atypia, so diagnostic excision or vacuum-assisted excision is usually recommended.
The lesion itself is benign but is regarded as a marker of modestly increased future breast cancer risk.
Preserved myoepithelial layer around entrapped tubules distinguishes it from tubular carcinoma histologically.
Careful radiological-pathological correlation is essential given the strong radiological overlap with malignancy.
reference.pathophysiology: A radial scar forms around a central zone of fibroelastic (fibroelastotic) tissue into which ducts and lobules are drawn and distorted, creating a stellate architecture with entrapped, sometimes distorted, tubules at the centre. The radiating arms show a range of proliferative changes including adenosis, ductal hyperplasia, cyst formation and papillomatosis. Although the process is benign and probably reflects a localised reparative or sclerosing response, the entrapment of tubules within dense stroma can mimic stromal invasion, and the associated proliferative epithelium may progress to atypical hyperplasia or carcinoma, explaining both the diagnostic difficulty and the increased cancer risk.
additionalDifferentials: Invasive carcinoma of no special type presenting as a spiculated mass
additionalInvestigations: Tomosynthesis to characterise the stellate lesion
Targeted ultrasound of the mammographic abnormality
Diagnostic surgical or vacuum-assisted excision for definitive assessment
Radiological-pathological concordance review at multidisciplinary meeting
redFlags: Associated atypical hyperplasia or in situ carcinoma on biopsy
Discordance between imaging and core biopsy findings
Increasing size or a developing palpable mass
Foci suspicious for tubular carcinoma at the lesion periphery
reference.prognosis: The radial scar itself is benign, and after appropriate excision the outlook is excellent. It signals a mild-to-moderate increase in long-term breast cancer risk, warranting continued participation in screening.
pitfalls: Confidently diagnosing malignancy on imaging alone, or conversely dismissing a spiculated lesion as benign
Relying on limited core biopsy that misses associated atypia or carcinoma
Misinterpreting entrapped tubules as invasive tubular carcinoma without myoepithelial stains
Neglecting ongoing surveillance given the increased future risk
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Breast Tumours (current edition)
Standard textbook of breast imaging on stellate lesions
management: Image-guided core or vacuum-assisted biopsy to sample the stellate lesion and detect associated atypia or malignancy
Diagnostic surgical or vacuum-assisted excision, because core sampling under-represents peripheral atypical hyperplasia, in situ or invasive carcinoma
Histological confirmation with myoepithelial immunohistochemistry to distinguish entrapped tubules from true stromal invasion
Escalation to the relevant oncological pathway if atypical hyperplasia or carcinoma is found at the periphery
Continued participation in mammographic screening given the modestly increased long-term breast cancer risk
Management within a breast multidisciplinary team combining radiology, surgery and pathology
